title: The Timing of Feedback After Success and Failure
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that the emotional aftermath of success or failure determines how well feedback lands, and that leaders often get the timing exactly backwards. After a win, people are relaxed and curious, making them receptive to critique they might otherwise resist. After a loss, the same feedback feels like an attack, even when well-intentioned. The article warns that leaders instinctively want to correct mistakes right after a poor showing, precisely when people are least able to absorb the lesson. It recommends capturing lessons from success immediately, while reserving post-failure conversations for encouragement first and analysis later, once the sting has faded.
points: People are more receptive to critical feedback right after a success than after a failure.
Leaders instinctively want to correct mistakes immediately after a weak performance, which backfires.
After a loss, people want encouragement and support before they want analysis.
Waiting a few hours or a day after a poor performance gives people the distance needed to hear feedback productively.
Capturing lessons in the glow of success helps people internalize what worked and why.
quotes: Criticism that follows a successful performance is accepted very differently than feedback offered after a sub-par performance.
After a successful outcome, people hear feedback more as a suggestion for improvement than as a piercing arrow aimed at their shortcomings.
They look to leaders for encouragement, not feedback, when they have experienced a defeat or failure.
By doing so, however, leaders unintentionally walk right into the lion's den, setting off a firestorm of protest and reaction in the process.
Because people are most open to feedback after success, leaders need to take advantage of the opportunity and offer observations that imprint what went right and why.
A few hours or a day later is plenty of time for everyone to gain some distance and begin the process of improving on a weak performance by dissecting what went south and why.
